issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette:
Priya's Vigilance

Priya Desai was thirty-two when the building collapsed. She had been attending a community forum on zoning ordinances at the Riverside Convention Center-a sprawling mid-century structure that city planners had been debating for months. As a relatively new member of the City Council, she had wanted to hear directly from constituents before the vote. She was standing near the entrance, speaking with a local business owner, when the sound came: not an explosion exactly, but a deep, structural groan, followed by a percussion of breaking concrete and rending steel that seemed to come from everywhere at once. The ceiling above the main hall gave way in a cascading collapse. Dust billowed through the corridors. For several seconds, Priya stood frozen, watching people run, hearing screams echoing off the remaining walls. She had turned and run toward what she thought was an exit, her heart hammering so violently she thought it might burst through her ribs. Later, she would learn that seventy-three people had died. She had been one of the last to leave that wing before it came down.

In the weeks immediately after, Priya functioned on adrenaline and shock. She attended the memorial services, gave statements to the press about structural safety oversight, pushed through council meetings with a kind of grim automaticity. But by the third week, something had shifted. She began to notice things: the way a heavy truck rumbling past her apartment made her stomach clench; the way she found herself studying the ceiling in any room, mentally tracing where a collapse might originate. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt almost factual, that the world was fundamentally more dangerous than she had previously understood. This wasn't a passing anxiety-it was a reorganization of her basic sense of safety. The building had been inspected, deemed safe, and had failed anyway. How many other structures harbored invisible weaknesses? How many other ordinary moments contained hidden catastrophe? The conviction settled into her like a stone: she could not trust what appeared solid.

This understanding of danger as omnipresent and unpredictable began to shape how Priya moved through her days. Because she was certain that constant vigilance was the only rational response to a world that could betray you without warning, she found herself scanning every room she entered-noting exits, assessing the integrity of walls and ceilings, positioning herself in spaces where she could see the most ground. At council meetings, she sat near the door. When she attended community events, her eyes moved in a restless circuit around the room, monitoring for threats. She became hyperaware of people around her, watching for signs of instability or danger in their faces and movements, though she could not have articulated what she was looking for. At night, the vigilance intensified. In her apartment, she felt exposed and vulnerable in ways that daylight seemed to mitigate. She found it harder to sleep, and when she did, her dreams were fractured and violent. She began checking the locks on her doors and windows multiple times before bed, a ritual that never quite satisfied the underlying sense of exposure.

The avoidance had accumulated gradually, almost without her noticing. She stopped going to unfamiliar restaurants or venues, reasoning that she couldn't properly assess the structural safety of buildings she didn't know. A colleague invited her to a new conference space downtown; Priya declined, claiming scheduling conflicts. She avoided situations that put physical stress on her body-she had always run in the mornings, but now the elevated heart rate and heavy breathing felt indistinguishable from panic, so she stopped. Yoga classes felt too vulnerable; the gym too unpredictable. When she did go out, she moved with a kind of tense efficiency, her body braced, her breathing shallow. Her hypervigilance toward people intensified alongside these physical restrictions. In council chambers, she found herself scrutinizing the structural engineers who presented reports, searching their faces for signs they were hiding something, that they, too, were complicit in a world of hidden dangers. Her staff noticed the change. Meetings that had once been collaborative became more tense; Priya asked more questions, demanded more assurances, seemed perpetually on edge. One of her longest-serving aides eventually transferred to another department, citing the constant pressure and surveillance.

What frightened Priya most now was the recognition that her vigilance, while exhausting, felt necessary-that without it, something terrible would surely happen. She had come to believe that she had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next, and this belief drove her to maintain her constant scanning, her avoidance of unfamiliar places, her physical withdrawal. But the vigilance itself had become a kind of prison. She was isolated, exhausted, and her work-the very thing that had drawn her to public service-had become a source of dread rather than purpose. Six months after the collapse, she finally reached out to a therapist, hoping that someone could help her understand how to live in a world that no longer felt survivable.
